\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{بگھارنا} (baghārnā)}{بگھارنا (baghārnā)}]{\ur{بگھارنا} (baghārnā) — to temper (with hot spiced oil)}

\label{lesson:UR-C508-bagharna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for to pat (into shape), then the Urdu for the heat of a flame.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{بگھارنا}}
\textbf{\ur{بگھارنا}} — \emph{baghārnā} — \textquotedblleft{}to temper (with hot spiced oil)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{امی} \ur{نے} \ur{زیرے} \ur{سے} \ur{دال} \ur{بگھاری۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ammī ne zīre se dāl baghārī.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Mum tempered the lentils with cumin.
\end{quote}

Past, with \ur{نے} (he or she …): \ur{اس} \ur{نے} \ur{دال} \ur{بگھاری}, \emph{us ne dāl baghārī}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{بگھارنا}} (\emph{baghārnā}) is inherited: CDIAL lists the Hindi cousin \emph{baghārnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to brown onions and spices in hot oil\textquotedblright{}, under Sanskrit \emph{vyaghārayati} (CDIAL 12191).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{baghārnā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{baghārnā}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ammī ne zīre se dāl baghārī.} — Mum tempered the lentils with cumin.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Urdu for to pat (into shape), then the Urdu for the heat of a flame, then say \emph{baghārnā} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ur{بگھارنا} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To temper (with hot spiced oil)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{بھوننا} (bhūnnā)}{بھوننا (bhūnnā)}]{\ur{بھوننا} (bhūnnā) — to roast; to brown (in a pan)}

\label{lesson:UR-C508-bhunna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for the heat of a flame, then the Urdu for to temper (with hot spiced oil).
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{بھوننا}}
\textbf{\ur{بھوننا}} — \emph{bhūnnā} — \textquotedblleft{}to roast; to brown (in a pan)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{اس} \ur{نے} \ur{کڑاہی} \ur{میں} \ur{مونگ} \ur{پھلی} \ur{بھونی۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{us ne kaṛāhī meṅ mūṅg phalī bhūnī.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
She roasted peanuts in the wok.
\end{quote}

Past, with \ur{نے} (he or she …): \ur{اس} \ur{نے} \ur{گوشت} \ur{بھونا}, \emph{us ne gosht bhūnā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{بھوننا}} (\emph{bhūnnā}) is probably inherited: CDIAL lists the Hindi cousins \emph{bhujnā} and \emph{bhūjnā}, \textquotedblleft{}fries, parches\textquotedblright{}, under Sanskrit \emph{bhṛjjati}, \textquotedblleft{}roasts\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 9583); the form \emph{bhūnnā}, with its \emph{-n-}, is not among its Hindi rows, so the link is likely rather than certain.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bhūnnā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bhūnnā}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{us ne kaṛāhī meṅ mūṅg phalī bhūnī.} — She roasted peanuts in the wok.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Urdu for the heat of a flame, then the Urdu for to temper (with hot spiced oil), then say \emph{bhūnnā} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{ڈھکن} (ḍhakkan)}{ڈھکن (ḍhakkan)}]{\ur{ڈھکن} (ḍhakkan) — a lid}

\label{lesson:UR-C508-dhakkan}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for to temper (with hot spiced oil), then the Urdu for to roast in a pan.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{ڈھکن}}
\textbf{\ur{ڈھکن}} — \emph{ḍhakkan} — \textquotedblleft{}a lid\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{دیگچی} \ur{کا} \ur{ڈھکن} \ur{کہاں} \ur{ہے؟}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{degchī kā ḍhakkan kahāṅ hai?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Where is the lid of the cooking pot?
\end{quote}

Masculine.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{ڈھکن}} (\emph{ḍhakkan}) is inherited from \emph{*ḍhakk}, \textquotedblleft{}cover\textquotedblright{}, a form CDIAL reconstructs, which also gives the Hindi cousin \emph{ḍhā̃knā}, \textquotedblleft{}to cover\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 5574).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ḍhakkan}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{degchī kā ḍhakkan kahāṅ hai?} — Where is the lid of the cooking pot?
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Urdu for to temper (with hot spiced oil), then the Urdu for to roast in a pan, then say \emph{ḍhakkan} again

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{ڈھانپنا} (ḍhāṅpnā)}{ڈھانپنا (ḍhāṅpnā)}]{\ur{ڈھانپنا} (ḍhāṅpnā) — to cover}

\label{lesson:UR-C508-dhanpna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for to roast in a pan, then the Urdu for a lid.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{ڈھانپنا}}
\textbf{\ur{ڈھانپنا}} — \emph{ḍhāṅpnā} — \textquotedblleft{}to cover\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{اس} \ur{نے} \ur{ڈھکن} \ur{سے} \ur{دیگچی} \ur{ڈھانپی۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{us ne ḍhakkan se degchī ḍhāṅpī.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}

Past, with \ur{نے} (he or she …): \ur{اس} \ur{نے} \ur{کھانا} \ur{ڈھانپا}, \emph{us ne khānā ḍhāṅpā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{ڈھانپنا}} (\emph{ḍhāṅpnā}) is inherited: CDIAL lists the Hindi cousin \emph{ḍhā̃pnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to cover\textquotedblright{}, under \emph{*ḍhapp}, a form it reconstructs (CDIAL 5579).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{کفگیر} (kafgīr)}{کفگیر (kafgīr)}]{\ur{کفگیر} (kafgīr) — a skimmer (a flat spoon)}

\label{lesson:UR-C508-kafgir}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for a lid, then the Urdu for to cover.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{کفگیر}}
\textbf{\ur{کفگیر}} — \emph{kafgīr} — \textquotedblleft{}a skimmer (a flat spoon)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{کفگیر} \ur{چولہے} \ur{کے} \ur{پاس} \ur{ہے۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{kafgīr chūlhe ke pās hai.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The skimmer is next to the stove.
\end{quote}

Masculine.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{کفگیر}} (\emph{kafgīr}) is usually traced to Persian \emph{kafgīr}, \textquotedblleft{}a skimmer\textquotedblright{}, built from \emph{kaf}, \textquotedblleft{}foam\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{gīr-}, \textquotedblleft{}to take\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kafgīr}, once more

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Urdu for a lid, then the Urdu for to cover, then say \emph{kafgīr} again
